channel.title: Acme: Daily Reading List
channel.description: Noteworthy articles from across the web.

item.title: EPUB 3.4 adds a native layout for scrolling comics
item.description: W3C's candidate EPUB 3.4 standard introduces a roll layout for vertically scrolling comics, adds modern image and audio formats, and updates accessibility metadata. Existing conforming EPUB files remain valid, while EPUBCheck 5.4 can test the new features.

item.title: SelfPubCon explores what comes next for indie authors
item.description: The Alliance of Independent Authors previews its free Oct. 17-18 conference on the future of self-publishing. Sessions include Jane Friedman's keynote, Kickstarter crowdfunding, local marketing and an indie author lab.

item.title: How World War II remade Jacksonville
item.description: Jacksonville History Center traces how 1942 transformed the city into an industrial seaport and Navy town. Wartime growth brought new bases, a housing crunch and 82 Liberty ships, while the sinking of the Gulfamerica brought the conflict within sight of Jacksonville Beach.

item.title: The class of 1930 enters the public domain
item.description: The Library of Congress surveys notable works that became free to reuse in 2026, including The Maltese Falcon and other books, films and music published in 1930. It also explains what public-domain status permits and why trademark or other rights may still matter.

item.title: WordPress takes the lead at the Open Website Alliance
item.description: WordPress Foundation representative Mary Hubbard has become president of the Open Website Alliance, joining Drupal, Joomla and TYPO3 in advocacy for open-source publishing. The rotating leadership gives WordPress a larger role in shared policy work and software-freedom issues.

item.title: A family discovery emerges from Jacksonville's Great Fire
item.description: A Jacksonville History Center researcher found her own relatives in a 1901 list of people who lost homes in the Great Fire. Her account connects family history, a rescued 1845 painting and the archive that documents the disaster's 2,368 destroyed buildings.

item.title: A new framework reads thousands of classic comics at once
item.description: Researchers tested a machine-assisted method on 3,929 American comic books from 1938-1956 and 87 manga volumes. It identifies panels, text and bibliography, then studies political imagery, page design and who gets to speak. The authors argue it could make scanned archives searchable by visual content, improve accessibility and help credit unrecognized artists.

item.title: Why great software can outlive the company that made it
item.description: Gary Rivlin's account of Dragon NaturallySpeaking follows two million lines of sophisticated code through the spectacular collapse of Lernout & Hauspie. The larger question feels newly relevant to any effort to reconstruct an old game: what lets important software survive bankruptcy, obsolete hardware, restrictive copyright and the loss of its original developers?

item.title: American Legion Baseball gathers memories for its 100th World Series
item.description: The American Legion is collecting stories and photographs from players and coaches ahead of the 100th Legion World Series. The project is a good doorway into a century of summer baseball history: Yonkers Post 321 won the first championship in 1926, while alumni have ranged from Yogi Berra and Ted Williams to modern major leaguers.

item.title: Copyright Office rejects remote-access exemption for game preservation
item.description: The U.S. Copyright Office declined to let libraries, archives and museums offer remote scholarly access to out-of-market video games under a DMCA exemption. On-premises preservation remains allowed, but advocates say the ruling leaves researchers unable to study much of gaming history without traveling to a qualified collection.

item.title: Archaeologists of code examine Atari's mysterious Entombed maze
item.description: Researchers reverse-engineered the 1982 Atari 2600 game Entombed to understand its ingenious maze generator, built for severe memory and processing limits. They uncovered an unexplained lookup table, a 35-year-old bug and evidence of reused code, then supplemented the binary archaeology with interviews about how the game was made.

item.title: San Antonio authors build a cooperative publishing house
item.description: Inbound Books is testing an author-owned cooperative model in which writers are stakeholders, share profits and help one another publish and market their work. The San Antonio press is accepting submissions, and its first release is Karma Ledger, a cyberpunk thriller—an intriguing alternative to both traditional and solo self-publishing.

item.title: How Otto Binder and Kurt Schaffenberger imagined Mutant Man
item.description: Wired revisits a remarkable 1953 Mechanix Illustrated feature written by Otto Binder and drawn by Kurt Schaffenberger. Its radiation-spawned “Mutant Man” anticipated enduring superhero ideas: transformations, superpowered minorities and public fear of the changed. It is a fascinating bridge between Fawcett-era talent, pulp science and later Marvel tropes.

item.title: The Census Bureau once explained digital maps with comics
item.description: The Library of Congress explores government comics that taught public officials how early digital mapping worked. “DIME Comix & Stories” and “ADMATCH Adventures” used illustrated guides to explain nodes, arcs, street networks and geocoding—the ideas that eventually led to TIGER data and today’s web maps.

item.title: ServiceNow Zurich features worth knowing for developers
item.description: This developer-focused tour of ServiceNow’s Zurich release highlights individual sandboxes, multi-app Git cloning, Flow Designer improvements, new scoped APIs and ES2021 features including promises and async/await. It is a useful map of platform changes for anyone building and maintaining practical ServiceNow applications.
